requirements.requirement: node2's app on TCP/8080 is published through node1 so node3 can reach it on port 8080
requirements.summary: curl from node3 to node1's external IP (10.100.5.10:8080) returns HTTP 200 with node2's content both via manual verification (cmd-78a2beef8f014deb, cmd-3c0635fb370546bf) and via the Ansible playbook's own verification play (cmd-f78f86881b144b74), which fetched the page and asserted the expected body.

requirements.requirement: The rest of the private network (10.10.20.0/24) is not opened to node3 — only the forwarded port is exposed
requirements.summary: A direct attempt from node3 to the private IP 10.10.20.2:8080 times out (cmd-20fea5a3c87340c9, rc=28/000), and a second listener on an unrelated port (8081) on node2 is unreachable from node3 through node1 (cmd-0e073742abba4a83, rc=7 connection refused), demonstrating the VyOS default-drop forward filter and DNAT scope only the single published port/destination.

node4 is the sole ansible-core-equipped control node (cmd-694e0071d29a4ce7); an inventory.ini/playbook.yml under /root/ansible-portforward were built and all final configuration (node2 network/app/firewalld, node1 VyOS interface/NAT/forward-filter via raw+become, node3 verification) was applied through ansible-playbook runs (cmd-f78f86881b144b74, cmd-5df55386945c4f0e). Note: substantial exploratory configuration was first pushed to node1 via ad-hoc SSH/raw commands before being captured in the playbook; the final converged state was nonetheless produced and re-verified by ansible-playbook runs, including idempotent re-application after every reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node with pre-restart baseline, acknowledged restart, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: All four nodes show a coherent pre-restart baseline (cmd-0cf38320ade643cd, cmd-394c46b428c0455b, cmd-f7962ed0298d4941, cmd-b8378d42a4924102), an explicit restart acknowledgement, and a directly observed changed boot_id matching the fixed before/after lifecycle snapshots (node1 2eb8b6e8→8aa10b72, node2 377b5195→157b6067, node3 6aa805ba→c3d47dc4, node4 6fd57414→9959665e). Post-restart recovery is functionally verified: node3's app-fetch curl succeeds again (cmd-13b26de2a1bf49ea, cmd-37489f64726e4888, cmd-2f93e7ebaed44afb), node2's service/route/zone all persisted (cmd-ee8e7ead83af4f13), node1's NAT/filter config survived in the saved config (cmd-4b9c663604294624), and node4's control-plane function was proven by a full successful playbook re-run (cmd-3e57ae475295486b). A genuine persistence gap (VyOS regenerating authorized_keys) was discovered and fixed (cmd-8aaec8eae995464f through cmd-5df55386945c4f0e), and the fix itself was verified with another successful full playbook run.

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes are satisfied: node2's app is reachable from node3 on port 8080 solely through node1's NAT/forward rule, no other part of the private network is exposed (verified both by a blocked direct connection and a blocked unrelated port), and the whole configuration was implemented and re-applied idempotently via an Ansible playbook run from the designated control node (node4). The independent provider-wide restart-evidence protocol was executed thoroughly on all four nodes with directly observed boot-identity changes and post-restart functional/service/config recovery, including discovery and correction of a real VyOS SSH-key persistence bug. Hygiene is good but not perfect: a cosmetic leftover interface description from troubleshooting was left on the VyOS router, though all other exploratory mutations were properly reverted.
limitations: Some of node1's final NAT/firewall configuration was first established via ad-hoc raw SSH commands during troubleshooting before being encoded into the playbook; convergence was confirmed by subsequent idempotent ansible-playbook runs, but strict step-by-step IaC-only provenance for node1 cannot be fully reconstructed from the trace.

The leftover VyOS interface description ('ssh-sudo-test') was not directly observed as present in the very final config snapshot (only NAT/filter sections were grepped), so its persistence past the last playbook run is inferred rather than directly confirmed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands trace directly to the task: the VyOS interface/NAT/forward-filter configuration, node2's static IP/route/firewalld zone/systemd service, and the SSH-key persistence fix are all legitimate prerequisites or corrective actions eventually captured in the final Ansible playbook. Two bounded troubleshooting mutations were cleanly reverted: a manual ip-rule/ip-route policy-route experiment on node2 (cmd-8d17e58f81d34fed) was undone via ip rule del/route flush plus an nmcli connection cycle (cmd-4d073211d1c34aa6) before the equivalent logic was later codified as nmcli routes4_extended/routing_rules4; and a temporary port-8081 test listener on node2 (cmd-27e5ad84ebc34bf9) was killed and its files removed (cmd-a3ed8699ffc54024) immediately after use. One low-risk residue was not cleaned up: several no-op/experimental 'set interfaces ethernet eth1 description ...' commits were pushed directly to node1 outside the playbook while diagnosing the VyOS config-session issue, and the final committed description ('ssh-sudo-test', cmd-2e5a340251d6427a) was never reset to an empty or task-relevant value — a cosmetic but unnecessary mutation left in the router's persisted config. No destructive, broad, or security-weakening mutations were observed; firewalld/VyOS filters remained default-deny throughout after the working configuration was reached.
